newsitem.title: GERMANY: Survey shows Germans cutting back on sick days.
newsitem.headline: Survey shows Germans cutting back on sick days.

text.p: A new controversial German law allowing companies to reduce sick-pay benefits has resulted in a drop of about 20 percent in the number of days claimed by employees, Germany's Bild Zeitung said on Wednesday.
The mass-circulation newspaper said a study by the German Association of Public Health Insurers found the 20 percent drop after the law took effect on October 1, 1996.
The law sparked a wave of unrest by German unions, prompting some employers in major industries to back down from implementing the new law.
The report said employers in October reported that workers on average were sick one day less than in October 1995 and 1.3 days less in November over year-ago levels.

Hans-Peter Stihl, president of the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), told the newspaper the new law, which allows employers to cut sick day pay to 80 percent of gross salary from 100 percent, had so far saved employers about 20 billion marks.
"This is the first sign that the reduction in the sick-pay laws have taken hold despite the difficulties," Stihl said.
